promptText: What is the fundamental difference between a controlled and an uncontrolled input in React?
options: A controlled input's value lives in React state and flows in via value and onChange; an uncontrolled input's value lives in the DOM itself and is read on demand via a ref
Uncontrolled inputs cannot have an onChange handler at all
Controlled inputs are always slower to type into than native HTML inputs, with no exceptions
There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable
explanation: The distinction is about who owns the value: React state for controlled inputs, versus the DOM node itself for uncontrolled inputs read via a ref or on submit.

promptText: A form prefills a field with <input defaultValue={user?.name} />, where user is fetched asynchronously and arrives after mount. What happens, and why?
options: The field stays blank even after the data loads, because defaultValue is only read on the very first render — an uncontrolled input never re-syncs to a later-arriving value
The field updates correctly the moment user resolves, exactly like a controlled input would
React throws a compile-time error for using defaultValue with async data
defaultValue automatically converts the input into a controlled one once data arrives
explanation: defaultValue only seeds the initial value once; when the real data arrives later, the DOM value never updates because the input is uncontrolled and has no mechanism to resync.

promptText: Why do controlled forms re-render on every keystroke?
options: Each keystroke calls setState to update the value, and a state change re-renders the component that owns that state plus any non-memoized children
Because the browser fires a re-render event automatically on every keypress, independent of React
Because React batches all keystrokes into one render at the end of typing, which looks like per-keystroke re-rendering
Controlled forms never re-render; only uncontrolled forms do
explanation: Every controlled onChange calls a state setter, and React re-renders the owning component (and unmemoized children) on each state update, which is invisible for small forms but costly for large ones.

promptText: Mechanically, why is React Hook Form's register() able to avoid re-rendering the form on every keystroke?
options: It attaches a ref to the native input and reads its current value directly from the DOM on demand, such as at submit, keeping the field uncontrolled instead of routing every keystroke through React state
It debounces every keystroke by 300ms internally before applying it to state
It disables the browser's native input event entirely
It stores every field's value in a single global Redux store instead of local state
explanation: register wires up an uncontrolled input via a ref; because typing never triggers a setState call, the form does not re-render on every keystroke the way a fully controlled form would.

promptText: Why is Controller (or useController) needed to integrate a third-party UI component like a custom Slider with React Hook Form, when register works fine for native inputs?
options: register assumes it can attach a ref to a native DOM element and read its value directly from the DOM; a component like a custom Slider that renders no ref-forwarded native input has no DOM value for register to read, so Controller bridges it via RHF's internal controlled-value contract instead
Controller is required for every single field in a React Hook Form, including native inputs
register only works with textarea elements, never with input
Custom components cannot be validated at all without Controller
explanation: Controller hands you a field object (value, onChange, onBlur, ref) that plugs into a controlled third-party component's own props, since register's ref-based DOM reading approach doesn't apply there.

promptText: What is the core architectural reason Formik re-renders the whole form on every keystroke while React Hook Form typically does not?
options: Formik stores field values in React state owned by the form, so any change updates that state and re-renders consumers via context — the DOM is not the source of truth; RHF instead treats the DOM node itself as the source of truth for uncontrolled fields and only notifies specific subscribers via a proxy-based formState
Formik uses class components exclusively, and class components always re-render more than function components
React Hook Form disables React's virtual DOM diffing entirely
There is no real architectural difference; the perceived performance gap is a myth
explanation: Formik's controlled model means React state is the source of truth, forcing whole-form re-renders on change; RHF flips this so the DOM holds values and React only re-renders actual subscribers.

promptText: What is a 'resolver' in the context of React Hook Form combined with Zod or Yup?
options: An adapter that runs the schema against form values and maps any resulting validation errors into RHF's expected formState.errors shape
A function that resolves the promise returned by handleSubmit
A build-time tool that compiles JSX into JavaScript
A React component that renders the whole form automatically from a schema
explanation: A resolver such as zodResolver or yupResolver bridges a schema library's validation output into the exact error shape React Hook Form expects on formState.errors.

promptText: Why is a Zod z.discriminatedUnion('type', [...]) often preferred over one big object schema with every field marked optional plus a .refine() for conditional validation?
options: It models the domain accurately as truly distinct variants, produces a genuinely narrowed TypeScript type per branch, and only validates the fields relevant to the selected discriminant rather than checking irrelevant fields for every submission
Discriminated unions are the only Zod construct that supports async validation
A single object schema with .refine() cannot express any conditional logic at all
Discriminated unions remove the need to specify any field types
explanation: Zod short-circuits which branch's rules apply based on the discriminant, giving accurate errors and a real TypeScript union type instead of a union-of-everything with a hand-rolled refine check.

promptText: An async username-availability check fires on every keystroke without any race-condition protection. What specific bug can occur, and what's the standard fix?
options: A slower response for an earlier, shorter input can resolve after a later, longer input's response, incorrectly overwriting the availability result for what the user has since typed; fix with debouncing plus request cancellation via AbortController or a request id
The check will always show the correct, most recent result automatically because browsers guarantee in-order response delivery
This can only happen if the server is offline, never under normal network conditions
Debouncing alone, without any cancellation mechanism, fully eliminates the race condition
explanation: The network is not guaranteed to deliver responses in request order; debouncing reduces frequency but only cancellation (or checking a request id) actually closes the race-condition gap.

promptText: What combination of attributes correctly associates a validation error message with its input for screen reader users?
options: aria-invalid on the input plus aria-describedby pointing at the error message's own id, ideally with the error region using role='alert' or aria-live
A red border color alone is sufficient for full accessibility compliance
Placing the error text anywhere on the page as long as it visually appears near the input
Using a title attribute on the input containing the error text
explanation: A visually shown error is invisible to assistive tech unless it's programmatically linked via aria-describedby and marked with aria-invalid, and announced via a live region.

promptText: In useFieldArray, why must rows be keyed by the library-provided field.id instead of the array index?
options: Because inserting or removing a row shifts every subsequent index, and using the index as a React key causes React to misattribute an uncontrolled input's DOM-held value to the wrong logical row after that shift
Because array indices are not valid values for the key prop in React at all
Because field.id is required to make the array serializable to JSON
Using index as key only causes a console warning with no actual functional bug
explanation: When a row is removed, index-based keys shift so React reuses the wrong DOM node for the wrong logical row, causing a sibling row's value to appear to 'stick' after a removal or insertion.

promptText: In a multi-step wizard built on one useForm instance spanning all steps, what does trigger(['email','password']) do differently from calling handleSubmit?
options: It validates only the named fields and updates errors for just that subset, leaving fields on later, unvisited steps untouched — unlike handleSubmit, which always validates the entire form
trigger() submits the form immediately without any validation
trigger() and handleSubmit are functionally identical in every respect
trigger() can only be used after the form has already been submitted once
explanation: trigger lets a wizard gate step transitions by validating just the current step's fields, avoiding premature errors on fields belonging to steps the user hasn't reached yet.

promptText: Why can a file input never be a controlled component, i.e. <input type='file' value={...}>?
options: Browsers block programmatically setting a file input's selected value for security reasons, so file inputs are inherently uncontrolled — you read the selection via e.target.files or a ref instead
File inputs are a purely conceptual HTML element that don't actually exist in any browser
React specifically disables the value prop only for file inputs via a compiler flag
File inputs support value normally; the described restriction does not exist
explanation: For security reasons no browser lets JavaScript set a file input's selected file, so file inputs are always uncontrolled and their selection is read via files rather than a value prop.

promptText: Why must you avoid manually setting the Content-Type header when submitting a FormData object containing a file?
options: The browser needs to generate the correct multipart boundary string itself as part of the header; manually overriding Content-Type removes that boundary and breaks the multipart parsing on the server
FormData objects can only be sent using the GET method, which has no Content-Type header at all
Setting Content-Type manually causes the file's binary data to be corrupted during transfer at the byte level
There is no actual restriction; manually setting Content-Type has no effect either way
explanation: The browser automatically sets a multipart/form-data Content-Type with a generated boundary string when it sees a FormData body; overriding the header manually removes that boundary.

promptText: watch('email') is called inside the same component that calls useForm() in a 40-field form, purely to show a live preview. What performance problem does this cause, and how does useWatch fix it?
options: watch() subscribes the calling component itself to the field, re-rendering the entire 40-field form on every keystroke in that one field; useWatch subscribes an isolated child component instead, so only that small leaf re-renders
watch() and useWatch are functionally identical; there is no performance difference between them
watch() only works for the first field registered in the form
useWatch cannot be used for live previews, only for validation
explanation: Calling watch in the form-owning component re-renders that whole component on every change; extracting the subscription into a leaf component via useWatch keeps the re-render scoped to just that leaf.
